PHASE 3 · ADVANCED HEALTH ASSESSMENT & CLINICAL DIAGNOSTICS

Week 48 — Lesson 72: Women’s Health & Gynecologic Assessment

FNP-level goal: Evaluate pelvic pain, abnormal uterine bleeding, vaginal symptoms, early-pregnancy concerns, contraception-related questions, and sexual-health presentations through stability, pregnancy status, inclusive history, focused examination, targeted testing, and safe disposition. Recognize ectopic pregnancy, hemorrhage, ovarian/adnexal emergencies, PID/tubo-ovarian abscess, severe infection, sexual violence concerns, and malignancy-risk presentations that cannot safely wait for routine follow-up.

Learning Objectives

  • Use pregnancy status and hemodynamic stability as early branch points in pelvic-pain and bleeding evaluation.
  • Build a differential for pelvic pain, abnormal bleeding, vaginal discharge, and genital lesions.
  • Perform or appropriately defer a trauma-informed, consent-based focused pelvic examination.
  • Recognize ectopic-pregnancy, hemorrhage, torsion/adnexal, PID, and sepsis red flags.
  • Select pregnancy testing, CBC, STI testing, urinalysis, ultrasound, and referral to answer a defined question.
  • Use confidential, nonjudgmental sexual history, safety screening, and closed-loop follow-up.

Part 1 — Stability and Pregnancy Status Come First

For patients with reproductive potential who have pelvic/abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, dizziness, syncope, shoulder pain, nausea/vomiting, urinary symptoms, or missed/abnormal menses, assess pregnancy possibility early. Measure vital signs and evaluate perfusion, severity/trajectory of bleeding, pain, mental status, and ability to tolerate oral intake. A positive pregnancy test with pain or bleeding requires attention to ectopic pregnancy and other pregnancy complications until location and stability are appropriately evaluated.

Sudden severe pelvic/abdominal pain, shoulder pain, fainting, weakness, hypotension, tachycardia, significant bleeding, peritoneal signs, or rapidly worsening symptoms can signal rupture/internal bleeding and needs emergency care. Contraception use, a recent normal-appearing period, or lack of known risk factors does not make pregnancy or ectopic pregnancy impossible. Do not delay emergency transfer to complete a routine office pelvic examination.

Part 2 — Build an Inclusive, Trauma-Informed History

Ask the patient how they describe their body, partners, and sexual practices. Explain why each question matters, protect confidentiality within applicable law, and avoid assumptions based on identity, relationship status, contraception, or pregnancy intention. Obtain menstrual and obstetric history: last menstrual period, cycle pattern, amount/timing of bleeding, pregnancy history/outcomes, contraception, recent emergency contraception, fertility treatment, prior ectopic pregnancy, pelvic surgery, endometriosis, fibroids, and cervical screening history.

For symptoms, clarify onset, location/laterality, sudden versus gradual pain, relation to intercourse/menses/bowel or bladder function, fever, discharge/odor, lesions, dyspareunia, urinary symptoms, GI symptoms, and prior episodes. Ask about STI risk and testing preferences without judgment. Offer appropriate privacy, chaperone availability, and the right to pause or decline any examination component. Consent is an ongoing process, not a one-time signature.

Part 3 — Pelvic Pain: A Differential That Protects Against Missed Emergencies

Pelvic pain may be gynecologic, urinary, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, neurologic, vascular, or pregnancy-related. Gynecologic considerations include ectopic pregnancy, pregnancy loss, ovarian torsion, ruptured/hemorrhagic cyst, PID/tubo-ovarian abscess, endometriosis, fibroids, and malignancy. Appendicitis, renal colic, pyelonephritis, diverticular disease, bowel disease, abdominal wall pain, and other processes remain in the differential.

Timing and laterality help but do not prove a diagnosis. Sudden severe unilateral pain with nausea/vomiting can raise concern for torsion or cyst complication; persistent lower-abdominal/pelvic pain with fever, discharge, cervical motion/uterine/adnexal tenderness, or STI risk can raise concern for PID. A benign initial examination does not exclude ectopic pregnancy, torsion, appendicitis, or evolving infection. Escalate when severity, instability, peritoneal findings, pregnancy status, or trajectory makes outpatient management unsafe.

Part 4 — Abnormal Uterine Bleeding: Define the Pattern and the Physiology

Document frequency, regularity, duration, amount, clots, intermenstrual/postcoital bleeding, bleeding after menopause, pain, pregnancy possibility, medications, anticoagulants, endocrine symptoms, weight change, bleeding/bruising history, and anemia symptoms. Clarify whether blood is vaginal/cervical/uterine, urinary, rectal, or from another source. Use a pad/tampon/cup history or patient’s own description rather than minimizing or assuming the amount.

Acute heavy bleeding with hypotension, tachycardia, syncope, chest symptoms, severe weakness, or evidence of major blood loss requires emergency evaluation and stabilization. In stable patients, pregnancy-related causes must be considered first when relevant. Structural, ovulatory/endocrine, iatrogenic, bleeding-disorder, infection, and malignancy causes are considered with age, history, examination, and testing. New bleeding after menopause, persistent unexplained bleeding, or cancer-risk context needs an appropriate gynecology pathway rather than repeated empiric hormonal treatment without reassessment.

Part 5 — Early Pregnancy and Ectopic Safety

Early pregnancy symptoms overlap with benign and nonpregnancy illnesses. When pregnancy is possible, a urine or serum pregnancy test is often an essential early diagnostic step. If pregnancy is confirmed and the patient has pain or bleeding, evaluate location, stability, and gestational context using the appropriate emergency/obstetric pathway. Ultrasound and quantitative hCG can contribute to assessment, but neither replaces emergency disposition when rupture or instability is possible.

Risk factors such as prior ectopic pregnancy, tubal/pelvic surgery, infertility treatment, PID, smoking, and certain reproductive histories can increase risk, but many ectopic pregnancies occur without recognized risk factors. Do not tell a patient with a positive pregnancy test and pain/bleeding to simply “repeat a test in a few days” unless an appropriate clinician-guided plan, access, and explicit emergency precautions are in place.

Part 6 — Vaginal Symptoms, Cervicitis, and STI Assessment

Discharge, odor, itch, burning, dysuria, dyspareunia, postcoital bleeding, and genital lesions have overlapping infectious and noninfectious causes. Ask about onset, color/amount/odor, products/irritants, medications, pregnancy, partner symptoms, barrier use, anatomic sites of exposure, and previous testing. A symptom description alone does not reliably identify a pathogen or exclude an STI.

Use site-appropriate testing, pregnancy status, examination, and local/current guidance to choose swabs, NAAT testing, microscopy, urine studies, and blood tests. STI testing can be confidential and should be offered without stigma. Treating a presumed yeast infection or UTI repeatedly without examination/testing can delay recognition of cervicitis, PID, dermatitis, genital herpes, malignancy, or another cause.

Part 7 — PID and Upper-Genital-Tract Infection

PID can present with pelvic/lower-abdominal pain, abnormal bleeding, dyspareunia, discharge, fever, cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, or adnexal tenderness. Findings may be mild or nonspecific, yet delayed recognition can harm reproductive health. Consider pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis, torsion, cyst, urinary disease, and other differential diagnoses at the same time.

Severe illness, fever, vomiting, inability to tolerate outpatient therapy, pregnancy, possible tubo-ovarian abscess, no response to treatment, hemodynamic concern, or uncertain diagnosis requiring urgent evaluation changes disposition. Follow current antimicrobial guidance and coordinate partner notification/testing/treatment and abstinence counseling as applicable; do not use this lesson as a substitute for current protocols.

Part 8 — Focused Pelvic Examination: Consent, Safety, and Limits

A pelvic examination is not required for every complaint and should only be performed with informed consent, privacy, correct equipment, and clinician competence. Explain the steps, invite questions, offer a chaperone, allow the patient to stop at any time, and document consent and limitations. Inspect external structures for lesions, trauma, discharge, erythema, and swelling. Speculum and bimanual findings, if performed, can assess bleeding source, discharge, cervix, uterine/adnexal tenderness, mass, and cervical motion tenderness.

Do not force an examination or let inability to perform it create false reassurance. If the patient declines, is too uncomfortable, is unstable, has severe pain, or needs a higher level of evaluation, use an alternative diagnostic/referral pathway. In a patient with suspected rupture, torsion, severe infection, or other emergency, disposition and stabilization are more important than a complete clinic examination.

Part 9 — Testing and Imaging: Ask a Clinical Question

Potential tests include pregnancy testing, CBC for anemia/infection context, type-and-screen in appropriate acute-care settings, urinalysis, STI testing, vaginal microscopy when available, and targeted endocrine/coagulation testing. Pelvic ultrasound can answer selected questions about pregnancy location, uterine/adnexal structure, free fluid, or mass. Imaging selection must reflect the patient’s stability, pregnancy context, symptom pattern, local resources, and clinical question.

A normal single test does not always end an evolving diagnosis. Track results, repeat or escalate when the timeline changes, and ensure the patient can access recommended imaging/specialty care. Do not use outpatient imaging orders as a substitute for emergency assessment in a patient with instability, suspected ectopic rupture, uncontrolled bleeding, severe infection, or peritoneal signs.

Part 10 — Preventive Care and Malignancy Safety

Assessment visits are opportunities to review pregnancy intention, contraception needs, cervical cancer screening status, breast symptoms, STI prevention/testing, vaccination, intimate-partner safety, and chronic-condition management. Preventive recommendations must be individualized to age, anatomy, risk, prior results, pregnancy, immune status, and current guidelines. Do not turn preventive screening into a reason to miss an acute symptom requiring diagnostic evaluation.

Persistent abnormal bleeding, postcoital bleeding, unexplained pelvic mass, persistent abdominal bloating/early satiety, persistent pelvic pain, new vulvar lesion, unexplained weight loss, or a concerning cervical/oral/breast finding requires timely diagnostic follow-up. “Normal screening in the past” does not explain a current concerning symptom.

Part 11 — Clinical Case: Pain, Bleeding, and a Positive Pregnancy Test

A 30-year-old has unilateral pelvic pain, light vaginal bleeding, dizziness, and a positive home pregnancy test. Blood pressure is borderline low.

FNP reasoning: pregnancy plus pain/bleeding and physiologic concern requires emergency ectopic-pregnancy evaluation. Do not reassure based on light bleeding or wait for a routine outpatient ultrasound.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: Fever, Pelvic Pain, and Discharge

A 24-year-old has lower-abdominal pain, dyspareunia, abnormal discharge, fever, and cervical motion tenderness on a consented examination.

FNP reasoning: PID is a high-priority consideration, while pregnancy-related and surgical alternatives remain important. Determine stability, pregnancy status, severity, ability to follow outpatient treatment, and whether urgent emergency evaluation is required.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: Heavy Bleeding and Anemia Symptoms

A 48-year-old reports weeks of progressively heavy irregular bleeding, fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and near-syncope. They have no confirmed pregnancy test and take an anticoagulant.

FNP reasoning: first assess hemodynamics and acute blood-loss/anemia risk, determine pregnancy status, and identify the bleeding source. Anticoagulation contributes to risk but does not explain away structural or malignant causes; emergency stabilization versus expedited gynecologic evaluation depends on physiology and severity.

FNP Women’s-Health Assessment Framework

  1. Assess stability and pregnancy early: vitals, perfusion, bleeding severity, pain trajectory, syncope, and pregnancy possibility.
  2. Use an inclusive history: menstrual, obstetric, sexual, medication, contraception, trauma/safety, and cancer-risk context.
  3. Build a broad differential: pregnancy-related, infectious, structural, endocrine/ovulatory, urinary, GI, surgical, and malignancy causes.
  4. Perform consent-based examination: explain, obtain ongoing consent, use a chaperone option, and document findings/limitations.
  5. Test with a question: pregnancy test, CBC, STI testing, UA, microscopy, ultrasound, and specialty pathway as indicated.
  6. Escalate red flags: positive pregnancy with pain/bleeding, shock/syncope, severe unilateral pain, peritoneal signs, uncontrolled bleeding, severe PID/systemic illness, or suspected torsion/abscess.
  7. Close the loop: results, partner/public-health steps when relevant, referral access, exact emergency precautions, and documented follow-up.

High-Yield Summary

Pelvic pain or bleeding: check pregnancy possibility early and assess stability before a routine outpatient differential.
Ectopic risk: positive test plus pelvic pain/bleeding, especially with severe pain, shoulder pain, dizziness, syncope, or instability, is an emergency pattern.
AUB: define timing/amount/source, assess acute blood loss and pregnancy, then evaluate structural, endocrine, medication, bleeding-disorder, infectious, and malignancy risk.
PID: can be mild/nonspecific; pain, tenderness, discharge, STI risk, fever, or systemic illness requires a thoughtful, current-guideline-based pathway.
Pelvic examination: requires consent, privacy, patient control, and clinician competence; inability to complete it does not make a dangerous diagnosis unlikely.
FNP standard: integrate physiology, pregnancy status, inclusive history, targeted testing, access to urgent care, result ownership, and explicit return precautions.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Gynecologic assessment, pregnancy testing, STI care, medication choices, imaging, referral, emergency disposition, and follow-up must follow current evidence, local protocols, scope requirements, and the individual patient’s presentation.
